    Latest Update: Air France-KLM Flying Blue — Monthly Promo Rewards

    📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2966 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Choosefi

    ⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.
    • A recurring monthly opportunity to book premium cabin flights at economy-level points pricing.
    • Picture this: you're reclining in Air France's La Première-adjacent Business cabin somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Champagne in hand, a three-course meal on the way, and a fully flat bed waiting for you after dinner.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

    A recurring monthly opportunity to book premium cabin flights at economy-level points pricing.

    Typical Promo Biz Class One-Way.

    Fuel Surcharges on Promo Awards.

    Picture this: you're reclining in Air France's La Première-adjacent Business cabin somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Champagne in hand, a three-course meal on the way, and a fully flat bed waiting for you after dinner. The couple in economy paid $900 for this flight. You paid 40,000 Flying Blue miles — points you transferred from your Chase Sapphire Reserve in seconds — and the cash value of what you're sitting in is closer to $2,500 to $6,000. That gap is the entire point. Air France-KLM's Flying Blue program runs what they call **Promo Rewards** — a monthly flash sale on award seats that slashes the points price by 25 to 50% on select routes. In Business class, that can mean seats that would normally cost 80,000+ miles dropping to as low as 40,000 miles one-way. On a route where a cash ticket retails for $3,000, you're extracting **7.5 cents per point** — and on premium routes during peak travel periods, that figure can climb to 15 cents per point. To put that in FI-community terms: the average point is worth 1 to 2 cents when redeemed for cash back or basic travel. This redemption can be worth 6 to 10 times that. If you have 40,000 transferable points sitting in a Chase or Amex account, this is the difference between a $400 economy ticket and a $3,000 business class experience — for the same points. The pricing inefficiency exists because Flying Blue uses these promotional awards as a marketing tool to fill premium cabin seats on specific dates that might otherwise go out with empty seats. Airlines would rather have a loyalist in that seat than fly it empty. You, as someone who's built a transferable points balance, are perfectly positioned to take advantage of the moment they make that trade-off. This isn't a loophole that's about to close. Flying Blue has run Promo Rewards consistently for years. It's a **structural feature of the program** — one the ChooseFI community can build an annual travel strategy around. The challenge isn't finding the deal. It's being ready when it drops.

    The mechanism behind Flying Blue Promo Rewards is elegantly simple once you understand it, and it separates this program from virtually every other airline loyalty play in your toolkit.

    Flying Blue Has a Dynamic Award Chart — With a Monthly Override.

    Flying Blue moved to dynamic pricing, which typically means the program is less predictable and often less valuable than the old fixed-chart days. But here's where it gets interesting: Promo Rewards operate as a fixed-price overlay on top of that dynamic system. On the 1st of each month (or within the first few days), Flying Blue publishes a curated list of routes — often 20 to 40 city pairs — with fixed, deeply discounted mile prices. Business class seats on transatlantic routes regularly appear at 40,000 to 50,000 miles one-way. These are not dynamic prices that will creep up as demand increases. They're locked promotional rates on specific routes.

    This means the program essentially gives you two separate games to play: the chaotic dynamic pricing game (usually skip it), and the monthly Promo Rewards game (always pay attention).

    The Fuel Surcharge Nuance You Must Know.

    According to recent reports, flying Blue does pass on carrier-imposed surcharges for standard awards on Air France and KLM flights — this can add $200 to $500 to what should be a points redemption. But here's the critical detail: Promo Reward bookings eliminate those surcharges. You pay the miles, a small booking fee, and that's it. This is a significant hidden value that casual points users miss entirely. The published cash price comparison becomes even more favorable once you factor in that you're not paying the surcharge on top.

    The Transfer Path Is Best-in-Class.

    Flying Blue partners with every major transferable currency at a 1:1 ratio:.

    Sources indicate that the instant transfer speeds from Chase, Amex, and Citi are critical here. When Promo Rewards drop and the best dates start disappearing within hours, you cannot afford a 3-day transfer window. If your points are in Chase or Amex, you can see a seat, transfer, and book in under 10 minutes.

    Routing Rules Give You Flexibility.

    It has been revealed that flying Blue allows open-jaw routing — meaning you can fly into Paris and out of Amsterdam (or vice versa) on a single award, letting you proposal a more dynamic European itinerary without paying for two separate tickets. The booking window opens at 359 days out, and miles are activity-based with a 24-month expiration window, so you're not racing against a clock as long as you keep your account active with occasional small transactions.

    It has been revealed that before the 1st of any month arrives, you need to be ready. Create a free Flying Blue account at flyingblue.com if you don't have one. More importantly, ensure your transferable points — Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Citi ThankYou, Capital One, or Bilt — are linked and ready. Don't transfer anything yet. You want to see the actual Promo Reward routes before moving a single point.

    When the list drops, you'll see a curated set of origin/destination city pairs with fixed Business class prices. Look for transatlantic routes from major U.S. gateways (New York, Los Angeles, Atlanta, Chicago, Miami) to European hubs like Paris (CDG) or Amsterdam (AMS).

    Go to flyingblue.com and use the award search tool. Enter your origin and destination from the Promo list. Switch the cabin to Business. Search across a 30-day window if possible — the calendar view shows you which dates have availability. Act within hours, not days. The best dates — particularly weekends, school holidays, and summer dates — disappear fast.

    It has been revealed that note: Flying Blue's search only reveals Air France and KLM metal for Promo Rewards. SkyTeam partner availability is separate and won't be Promo-priced.

    Do not transfer points yet. Confirm the exact flights, dates, and total miles cost. Take a screenshot. Note the flight numbers and times. Availability can disappear between the moment you see it and the moment you book, so move quickly through the next steps.

    From your bank portal (Chase, Amex, Citi), initiate the transfer to Flying Blue. For Chase, Amex, and Citi, transfers are instant. Capital One and Bilt take 1–2 days, so these are less ideal for Promo Rewards' speed-dependent window. Transfer exactly what you need — Promo award prices are fixed, so there's no cushion math required.

    With miles in your account, return to the award search, re-confirm your dates are still available, and book. You'll pay the fixed Promo miles price plus taxes and fees (minimal, with no fuel surcharges on Promo awards). You'll receive a confirmation email immediately.

    Don't panic. Wait for next month. Or search the current month's Promo list for alternative routes — sometimes less popular city pairs have excellent availability. You can also check if the same route appears at standard dynamic pricing, but compare the CPP carefully before transferring for a non-Promo redemption.

    Flying Blue moved to dynamic award pricing, which normally makes costs unpredictable and often unfavorable. But the Promo Rewards program creates a monthly fixed-price override on select routes that dramatically undercuts the dynamic system. Each month, Flying Blue publishes a curated list of discounted routes with pricing 25 to 50 percent below standard and with fuel surcharges eliminated entirely. This creates a repeatable, predictable opportunity cycle: check on the 1st, find a discounted route, transfer points instantly from Chase or Amex, and book before the best dates are taken. The structural advantage is that most casual travelers do not know about Promo Rewards or do not act fast enough — which leaves more availability for prepared ChooseFI community members who treat the 1st of each month as a mini-booking event.

    Industry observers note that card links may earn ChooseFI a commission. See our advertiser disclosure.

    Let's walk through a redemption that the ChooseFI community has actually executed.

    The Route: New York (JFK) → Paris (CDG) in Business class on Air France.

    It has been revealed that the Cash Price: A direct Air France Business class ticket on this route typically retails between $3,000 and $5,500 depending on the season. For this example, let's use a realistic mid-range price of $3,800.

    The Promo Reward Price: 40,000 Flying Blue miles one-way, plus approximately $60–$80 in taxes and fees. No fuel surcharges — because it's a Promo award.

    It has been revealed that the CPP Calculation: $3,800 ÷ 40,000 miles = 9.5 cents per point. That's nearly 10x what you'd get using those same Chase points for cash back at 1 cent each.

    You board at JFK and step into Air France's Business class cabin — the same product that Business travelers are paying $3,800+ to access. You have a lie-flat seat with direct aisle access, a curated French menu with Champagne service before takeoff, noise-canceling headphones, an amenity kit, and pajamas on longer segments. The CDG lounge is yours before departure — the Air France lounge in Terminal 2E is a genuine culinary experience, not an airport afterthought. You land in Paris rested, not wrecked.

    Industry observers note that for a couple, you'd need 80,000 miles total — both ways would be 160,000 miles. A pair of Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve cardholders who signed up in the same year could realistically have this banked between welcome bonuses and everyday spend. Transfer from Chase to Flying Blue: instant. Time from decision to booking: under 15 minutes.

    Industry observers note that you did not pay $7,600 for two Business class tickets across the Atlantic. You paid 80,000 points and roughly $160 in fees. Those points cost you, at most, $800 in credit card spend if you valued them at 1 cent each — meaning you captured $7,440 in travel value from an $800 equivalent investment in points. That's the FI multiplier that makes this program worth mastering.

    According to recent reports, ready to unlock a world of free travel? Start with the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card.

    Do This: Set a Monthly Calendar Reminder for the 1st.

    Industry observers note that flying Blue Promo Rewards are time-sensitive by design. The best routes with the best dates are gone within 24–48 hours of announcement. Put a recurring reminder on your calendar. Treat the 1st of each month like a mini-event.

    Do This: Keep a Points Buffer in Your Transferable Accounts.

    Because Promo Rewards require fast action and the best transfer partners (Chase, Amex, Citi) are instant, you want at least 40,000–80,000 points already sitting in your transferable account before the announcement. Don't be in a position where you need to wait on a credit card statement to close before you can transfer.

    Do This: Use Open-Jaw Routing to Maximize Your Trip.

    Flying Blue allows open-jaw routing. Book into Paris (CDG) and out of Amsterdam (AMS) — or any combination of Air France/KLM hub cities — and you've just built a multi-country European trip into a single award booking. This is the kind of routing flexibility that turns a one-city trip into a proper adventure.

    Do This: Track Multiple Months of Route Patterns.

    In a recent development, promo routes rotate monthly, but certain routes appear repeatedly — particularly transatlantic and routes between European hubs and Africa or the Middle East. After 2–3 months of observation, you'll start to recognize patterns and can plan your travel around routes that are likely to repeat.

    Avoid This: Transferring Points Before Confirming Availability.

    This is the single biggest mistake beginners make. Always confirm the specific flight, date, and cabin availability before transferring points. Miles are a one-way street — you cannot transfer them back. If availability disappears after you've transferred, you're left with Flying Blue miles that may not be useful for your target route at standard (non-Promo) pricing.

    Avoid This: Ignoring Standard Award Pricing.

    According to recent reports, flying Blue's dynamic pricing outside of Promo Rewards can be punishingly expensive. A Business class seat that costs 40,000 Promo miles might cost 90,000+ miles at standard dynamic pricing. Always wait for the Promo if you can — patience pays.

    According to recent reports, the ideal earning setup for this redemption combines a Chase Sapphire Reserve (3x on travel and dining, instant transfer to Flying Blue) with an Amex Gold or Platinum (4x on dining/groceries or 5x on flights respectively, also instant transfer). Between two cards, you can accumulate 40,000–80,000 points in a single year of normal household spending.

    Best For: Flexible Couples and Solo Travelers Who Blueprint in Advance.

    This redemption is purpose-built for the FI community member who thinks in systems, not spontaneous splurges. You're someone who has already built a transferable points balance of at least 40,000–80,000 points across Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, or Citi ThankYou — and who can act decisively when the right route appears.

    Sources indicate that couples are the sweet spot. Two people, two Business class seats, one incredible transatlantic experience. Solo travelers benefit enormously too — a single seat at 40,000 miles is one of the highest-CPP solo redemptions in the entire transferable points ecosystem.

    Recent findings suggest that minimum Viable Setup: 40,000 Flying Blue miles or 40,000 transferable points in Chase, Amex, or Citi. A Flying Blue account with verified transfer links. The flexibility to travel within a 30-day window of whatever routes appear that month.

    Create a free Flying Blue account at flyingblue.com and enable email notifications. Keep at least 40,000 to 80,000 transferable points in your Chase, Amex, Citi, Capital One, or Bilt account. Set a recurring calendar reminder for the 1st of each month.

    Industry observers note that visit flyingblue.com on the morning of the 1st (or within the first few days) to see the new Promo Rewards routes. Scan for destinations that match your interests. Note the discounted mile pricing and travel date windows — promos typically cover travel within the next 2 to 3 months.

    Use the Flying Blue award search to check specific dates on the promo routes in business class. Confirm that seats are available at the promo price before you transfer any points. The calendar view lets you scan across multiple dates swiftly.

    In a recent development, transfer the required miles from Chase (instant), Amex (1-2 days), Citi (instant), Capital One (1-2 days), or Bilt (1-2 days). Book on flyingblue.com the moment your miles arrive. Do not wait — promo availability is limited and the best dates disappear within hours.

    Recent findings suggest that promo Rewards typically offer 25 to 50 percent off standard dynamic pricing. A business class transatlantic award that normally costs 80,000 to 100,000 miles one-way can drop to 40,000 to 50,000 miles on a Promo Reward. Additionally, fuel surcharges are eliminated on promo awards, saving another $100 to $300 per ticket that would otherwise be charged on standard awards.

    It has been revealed that chase Ultimate Rewards and Citi ThankYou are the best because they transfer instantly to Flying Blue at a 1:1 ratio. Amex Membership Rewards and Capital One both transfer at 1:1 but take 1 to 2 business days. Bilt also transfers at 1:1. Since promo availability is time-sensitive, instant transfer partners give you a meaningful speed advantage.

    According to recent reports, yes. Promo Rewards rotate destinations each month and cover specific travel date windows, typically 2 to 3 months out. You cannot choose which routes are discounted. The strategy works best for travelers who have a list of destinations they want to visit and can match those against whatever promos appear each month rather than needing a specific route on a specific date.

    Recent findings suggest that the best routes with the best dates typically sell out within 24 to 48 hours of the monthly announcement. Business class availability is particularly limited. Set a reminder for the 1st of each month and check within the first few hours of the announcement for the widest selection of dates and routes.

    This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

    Flying Blue Promo Rewards is the most repeatable sweet spot in travel rewards because it renews every single month. While other sweet spots are one-time plays or annual opportunities, Promo Rewards gives you 12 chances per year to book premium cabin flights at 25 to 50 percent off standard pricing with no fuel surcharges. The system rewards exactly the kind of behavior the FI community already excels at: preparation, patience, and decisive action when the numbers align. Keep 40,000 to 80,000 transferable points in reserve, check on the 1st of every month, and book the moment you find a route that matches your travel list. Over time, this single strategy can deliver thousands of dollars in business class experiences at economy-level points costs.

    #136988. Retired Man Tries to Spend More Money, Mostly Fails

    📅 16 Jan 2025 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1493 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mrmoneymustache ↗ Open Full Page

    Retired Man Tries to Spend More Money, Mostly Fails

    📅 16 Jan 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1493 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Money Mustache lost some credibility among the faithful when he wrote this blog post about actually trying to spend a bit more money, while buying a Tesla as the first step in that program.
    • “I’m such an enlightened middle-aged Badass, adjusting habits and realigning myself at the snap of my fingers.
    • Industry observers note that so, two years passed with an even greater feeling of abundance.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A couple of years ago, Mr. Money Mustache lost some credibility among the faithful when he wrote this blog post about actually trying to spend a bit more money, while buying a Tesla as the first step in that program.

    I thought to myself at the time,.

    “I’m such an enlightened middle-aged Badass, adjusting habits and realigning myself at the snap of my fingers. Onward to the next forty eight years of the Good Life!”.

    Industry observers note that so, two years passed with an even greater feeling of abundance. I had a marvelous time traveling everywhere and spending money like I thought a proper wealthy person would do.

    I dined out in stylish restaurants, booked hotels based on their niceness rather than their cheapness, paid extra to sit in the “reduced torture” seats of the airplanes, and gave zero fucks about paying double for groceries if I happened to be in a Whole Foods rather than my usual Sam’s Club and Costco (and yes I treat myself to memberships at both warehouse stores!).

    According to recent reports, among the highlights, my son and I have worked our way though a nice selection of late night EDM concerts and three Meowwolf art venues including a Christmas Day road trip from our winter home in Tempe Arizona to Las Vegas last year. And having spent much of the year as a single man, I had a wide open schedule to just meet up with friends, explore latest places and meet new people as opportunities came up. It felt like a year of adventurous transition, which means it felt like much more than twelve months.

    With all this flashy spending, I was sure my budget must have crept back into full American Consumer territory. But I was having too much fun to bother adding it all up to check.

    Until recently, when I was doing another round of informal coaching for a friend and we both decided to tally our spending for the past year to compare notes.

    When I finally finished sorting all of those transactions into a spreadsheet and hit the “sum” button, the results surprised me.

    It has been revealed that while my overall spending had indeed increased (especially in travel-related categories), the big-picture effect was still pretty minimal. Depending on how I account for things like the car and my business expenses, my spending went from $20,000 to about $30,000 (plus the usual hidden subsidy of a paid-off house.).

    According to recent reports, this level could still be sustained by a $1 million investment nest egg. Since my investments are quite a bit higher than that (especially after these recent years of crazy economic growth and the never-ending stock market rally), I’m still way under budget.

    Although I still “failed” to really increase my spending to the MMM-recommended levels for old wealthy people, this still makes me happy, because I have genuinely had more fun with the abundance mindset, and I can keep trying more life experiments in the coming years.

    In a recent development, as we covered in the 2019 article on the idea of an Optimization Council, it’s always a good idea to compare our spending, tips and tricks on how to get the most out of life. Almost twenty years into early retirement, this is where I have landed so far, although I’m always learning and open to feedback.

    Anyway, let’s cut the wistful commentary and get into the budget.

    In summary: Wow, how interesting! When we compare this to my 2019 post on that year’s spending, it’s only a bit higher even after all the inflation we have seen in recent years. I spent more on travel and fun, but less on home renovation – partly because I was away so much I didn’t have as much time to work on my house. The health insurance is a upcoming cost too since I was self-insured back then.

    My budget is notably missing the biggest expense for most people, which is housing costs. This is because I paid off my house long ago, and I also love working on and taking care of my own home, which means there are no bills for lawn mowing, plumbers, tree pruning or handyman services.

    In a recent development, this strategy is not for everyone, and it’s not even the optimum financial one for me – I would have been better off taking out the biggest mortgage I could get at 3% back in the sweet borrowing times of 2021, and putting all that principal to work in stock index funds where it would have almost doubled since then. But I still get a great peace of mind from just having no mortgage payment, and there’s really no better way to use your money than to buy such good feelings. Also, I get a secondary benefit of not having to buy house insurance, which saves me another $2000 per year, boosting my effective return on that payoff.

    Industry observers note that first of all, the biggest money saving factor of good health and good luck has continued, meaning I’ve still had no actual medical expenses. But I still do maintain two layers of health care support which together feel very much like the ultimate version of health insurance: a membership with a top of the line Direct Primary Care (DPC) medical clinic ($107 per month) plus a high-deductible plan ($201) with a health sharing organization called Sedera.

    The combined cost of $308 per month is less than the cheapest Bronze initiative in the field of standard health insurance, yet I get personalized support with zero deductible for almost all typical medical needs, plus some protection from larger medical bills if my good luck runs out.

    In a recent development, but as a disclaimer, I’m not an expert on medical needs and health insurance because I’ve had so little experience with the system. And the highest priority in my life is arranging my days for maximum health to give me the best chance of keeping it this way.

    When it comes down to it, money is a tool for survival and if we’re lucky, self actualization. So I’m always asking myself if there’s anything I can change or improve to make the most of this good fortune.

    I also try to keep in mind an interesting principle of happiness, which claims that,.

    Fixing your persistent problems is more effective than just doubling down on things that are already good in your life.

    For me, there are already a lot of good things which don’t need improving. My family, friends, relationships, health, food and daily activities are pretty much as good as I could imagine.

    Sources indicate that the only annoyance I can think of is physical chaos: I have a lot of space-intensive hobbies like construction and music, and I presently live in a pretty small house which is basically maxed out. I could really use a doubling of my workshop space from the current 2-car, 440 square foot garage to maybe a thousand or so.

    Sources indicate that but I also love where I live and wouldn’t want to give up my views, neighbors or current place. So I’ll keep optimizing what I’ve got unless some perfect opportunity comes up for a bigger place right on my block.

    It has been revealed that in the longer run, a mountain compound with its own cliffs and stream are also on my “maybe” list. But once again, my days and life are already overbooked with joyful things. My existing house and our HQ Coworking space already have long to-do lists. Would I actually be happier if I added another place to my portfolio? So I keep this idea on the shelf until I’m willing to trade it for another existing commitment – like selling my house or the coworking space.

    But for now, I’m just extremely excited to blaze into 2025 with loads abundance and piles of challenging stuff on my to-do list. And I wish you the same!

    In the Comments: Where are you at on this spectrum of stinginess versus abundance mentality, and fulfilment versus longing in life?

    A Temporary Note about Teslas and other electric cars:Rumor has it that the $7500 EV tax credit might be disappearing when our newly introduced president takes over next week, so this might be the cheapest chance to buy what I feel are the best cars on the market: The Model Y, or Model 3.

    Both used and fresh prices are at record lows so shop around and get an additional $1000 off a new one if you use a referral code from a friend or here’s mine if you need one (many thanks!)Full article here at The Model Y Experiment.

    Figure’s HELOC suits homeowners who want a lump sum within days, since the whole line is drawn at closing, but its annual percentage rate (APR) leaves out the origination fee, up to 4.99% of that draw. By our math, a 4.99% fee on a 10-year line at 8% equals about 1.2 percentage points of APR, so a bank line with no closing costs is cheaper unless its APR is over 1.2 points above Figure’s.

    Borrowers who will spend the whole amount at once, such as paying off credit cards, get a fixed rate and can have the money in as few as five business days. Anyone who wants to draw in stages or pay the least overall should compare home equity lines that charge no closing costs and let you borrow as you go.

    Aeroplan Stopovers — Two Cities for the Price of One

    📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2862 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Choosefi

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.
    • One of the highest-value redemptions in travel rewards.
    • Sources indicate that picture this: you're settling into a lie-flat business class seat somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of something cold in hand, knowing that in 48 hours you'll be waking up in Istanbul — and then, a few days later, continuing onward to Bangkok.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

    One of the highest-value redemptions in travel rewards.

    Sources indicate that picture this: you're settling into a lie-flat business class seat somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of something cold in hand, knowing that in 48 hours you'll be waking up in Istanbul — and then, a few days later, continuing onward to Bangkok. Two bucket-list cities. One award booking. One points balance. This is what the Aeroplan stopover sweet spot feels like in practice. It's not a trick or a loophole — it's a deliberately designed feature of Air Canada's Aeroplan program that the vast majority of travelers simply don't know exists. And that gap between awareness and reality is exactly where the ChooseFI community finds its edge. Here's the math that should make your jaw drop. A business class itinerary from North America to Istanbul with a continuing flight onward to Bangkok — two long-haul segments, lie-flat seats, Star Alliance lounges at every connection — would cost somewhere between **$6,000 and $15,000 in cash**. That's a realistic retail range depending on season and how far out you book. Most people never consider it a possibility for a family vacation or a milestone trip because the sticker price puts it in a different universe. With Aeroplan, you're booking that same itinerary — the same seats, the same lounges, the same Turkish Airlines or Thai Airways product — for **75,000 Aeroplan points**. At the low end of the cash price range, that's already **8 cents per point**. At the high end, you're extracting **20 cents per point** from a currency that most people earned by putting groceries on a credit card. The pricing inefficiency here is structural. Aeroplan's partner award chart prices long-haul business class at a fixed rate regardless of cash fare fluctuations. When business class prices spike — around holidays, during peak travel seasons, during major events — your points cost stays exactly the same. You're insulated from the market. That's the FI mindset applied to travel: you've already paid for the trip in points, slowly accumulated through everyday spending, and now you're simply redeeming the stored value. The stopover itself is nearly free. Aeroplan charges just 5,000 extra miles to add a stopover city to a one-way award. That means your Istanbul layover becomes a multi-day stay — at zero additional points cost beyond that small add-on — and you haven't booked a second award at all. One booking. Two destinations. That's the entire premise, and once you see it, you can't unsee it.

    The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegantly simple once you understand it, but it requires knowing three things that most travelers don't: how Aeroplan's routing rules work, what a stopover actually is in the context of an award ticket, and why Star Alliance's global network makes this scalable to almost any destination pair you can imagine.

    When Aeroplan relaunched its loyalty program in 2020, it did something remarkable: it eliminated fuel surcharges entirely and published a partner award chart with fixed pricing for flights on Star Alliance carriers. This is critical. When you book Turkish Airlines business class through Aeroplan, you pay the Aeroplan fixed chart rate — not what Turkish Airlines would charge in its own currency or miles program, and not the inflated cash price. That fixed chart is the engine of this redemption.

    For long-haul international business class, Aeroplan's chart prices routing through multiple regions based on your origin and destination — not every intermediate stop. This is the aha moment. Aeroplan determines your award price based on where your journey starts and where it ends, and then allows you to add a stopover in between for just 5,000 additional miles. The stopover city is priced as a pass-through for the purpose of calculating your award zone, not as a second trip.

    On a one-way Aeroplan award, you're permitted to add a free stopover — meaning you can stay in an intermediate city for any length of time before continuing to your final destination. That 5,000-mile add-on is essentially the cost of a full additional destination. Compare that to booking a second one-way award from Istanbul to Bangkok, which would cost you another 40,000–55,000 Aeroplan points in business class. The math is decisive.

    The routing must be geographically sensible — you can't fly backwards across the globe — but Aeroplan's allowance for multi-segment itineraries through Star Alliance hubs gives you enormous flexibility. Istanbul (IST) is a Turkish Airlines hub. Bangkok (BKK) is served by Thai Airways and several Star Alliance carriers. Both are Star Alliance partners. Both are bookable through Aeroplan at fixed chart rates with no fuel surcharges.

    The best part for the ChooseFI community is how accessible the underlying points are. Aeroplan accepts transfers from four major programs:.

    Chase's instant transfer speed is particularly valuable here. When you find business class availability — which can disappear quickly — you want to move points immediately. Having Chase Ultimate Rewards as your primary earning currency means you can search, find space, and transfer points before the availability window closes. The 1:1 ratio across all four programs means no conversion math — every point you earn translates directly to one Aeroplan mile.

    Booking an Aeroplan stopover award in business class is genuinely one of the more complex redemptions in the travel rewards world, but it becomes manageable when you break it into distinct phases. Here's exactly how to do it.

    According to recent reports, start by deciding on your two destinations. Aeroplan stopovers work best when your intermediate city is a major Star Alliance hub that lies geographically between your origin and final destination. Classic combinations include North America to Istanbul (Turkish Airlines hub) continuing to Southeast Asia, or North America to a European hub continuing to the Middle East or East Africa. Your stopover city should be somewhere you genuinely want to spend 2–5 days — this is a real trip, not just a layover.

    In a recent development, this is the most important and most time-consuming step. You need to find saver-level business class availability on both segments independently before you book.

    Once you've confirmed availability on both segments, go to aeroplan.com and use the multi-city search function. Enter your full itinerary — origin, stopover city with your intended layover dates, and final destination.

    Once you've confirmed the award is bookable and are ready to complete the reservation:.

    Recent findings suggest that complete your booking on aeroplan.com or with a phone agent, confirm the stopover is properly reflected in your itinerary, and save every confirmation email. Verify your seats on each carrier's website immediately after booking.

    A stopover is an intentional break in your journey lasting more than 24 hours at a connecting city. Most airlines treat stopovers as separate tickets, charging full price for each segment. Aeroplan is one of the few programs that allows a free stopover on round-trip awards, letting you explore a connecting city for days before continuing to your final destination. This is fundamentally different from a layover, which is a brief connection of a few hours at an airport. The stopover must be in a city served by a Star Alliance carrier on your routing, and the key is that Aeroplan prices the entire itinerary as one award, not two.

    Recent findings suggest that card links may earn ChooseFI a commission. See our advertiser disclosure.

    Let's build a real example so you can see exactly what this looks like on paper — and in the air.

    The Route: Toronto (YYZ) → Istanbul (IST, 4-day stopover) → Bangkok (BKK) The Carrier: Turkish Airlines business class on both segments The Points Cost: 75,000 Aeroplan miles for the two segments + 5,000 miles for the stopover = 80,000 Aeroplan miles total Cash Equivalent: A comparable business class itinerary on this routing typically retails for $9,000–$12,000 in 2026, depending on when you search and how far in advance you book.

    The CPP Calculation: At the midpoint cash value of $10,500 against 80,000 points, you're extracting 13.1 cents per Aeroplan mile — well inside the 8–20 cent range this sweet spot delivers, and roughly 10–13 times the value of redeeming Aeroplan miles for cash back.

    The Turkish Airlines business class product on long-haul routes is consistently rated among the top business class experiences in the Star Alliance network. On the YYZ–IST segment — operated on a 787 or A330 — you'll have access to a lie-flat seat with direct aisle access, the Turkish Airlines Lounge in Istanbul (widely considered one of the best airport lounges in the world, full stop), and a meal service that reflects the airline's culinary reputation. The IST lounge alone — with its restaurant, spa, golf simulator, and sleeping areas — is worth lingering in even before your onward connection.

    In Istanbul, your four days might include the Hagia Sophia at sunrise, a Bosphorus dinner cruise, and the Grand Bazaar before you head to the airport to continue your journey. You've paid nothing additional for this stay beyond the 5,000-mile stopover fee.

    The IST–BKK segment puts you into Bangkok in the evening, ready for Thailand's extraordinary food, culture, and cost of living — which, for the FI-minded traveler, means your lodging and meals on the ground are remarkably affordable, stretching the value of your trip even further.

    Sources indicate that total points cost for two lie-flat business class segments and a full European city stay: 80,000 miles, earned on everyday credit card spending. That's the entire proposition, and those numbers are real.

    Book at exactly 355 days out. Aeroplan opens its booking window at 355 days before departure. The best business class availability on popular routes — especially Turkish Airlines long-haul — appears at this window and gets claimed promptly. Set a calendar reminder and be ready to search at the 355-day mark for your target travel dates.

    According to recent reports, use Chase Ultimate Rewards as your primary earning currency for this redemption. The instant transfer speed to Aeroplan is genuinely differentiating. When you find award space and need to move promptly, Chase lets you transfer and book in the same session. Amex, Capital One, and Bilt all require 1–2 days, during which your availability can evaporate.

    Recent findings suggest that search availability before you transfer points. Confirm space exists on every segment before a single point moves. There's no undo button on a transfer, and Aeroplan points sitting idle in your account are fine — points transferred to an account where you can't find availability are a headache.

    In a recent development, call Aeroplan for complex routings. The online multi-city tool is functional but can struggle with nuanced stopover configurations. Phone agents are experienced with these bookings and have the same access to inventory. The call is worth it for an $80,000-point booking.

    Recent findings suggest that leverage the open-jaw rule too. Aeroplan also allows open-jaw routing — fly into one city, depart from another. Combined with the stopover, you can design a route that visits three geographic points on a single award: fly into Istanbul, take trains or ferries to Athens, and fly home from Athens. The award prices the same way.

    Industry observers note that don't assume partner availability matches Aeroplan's search. Turkish Airlines and other Star Alliance partners don't always make every seat available through Aeroplan's online portal. If you see space on the carrier's own site but not on aeroplan.com, call — agents can often access inventory the website misses.

    Don't book inflexible connecting flights. Long-haul itineraries with tight connections are a risk. Build in at least a 3-hour connection at hub airports to protect against irregular operations that could affect your award segments.

    Don't earn Marriott Bonvoy® points with this redemption in mind. The 3:1 transfer ratio to Aeroplan makes Marriott a poor choice for funding this specific award. Stick to Amex, Chase, Capital One, or Bilt at 1:1.

    According to recent reports, don't book this for a time-sensitive trip. Award availability, transfer timelines, and multi-carrier coordination mean this requires planning runway. Build in at least 3–4 weeks of lead time beyond the actual booking date.

    This redemption is purpose-built for the advanced travel rewards enthusiast in the ChooseFI community — someone who has already mastered the basics (earning transferable points, understanding award charts, booking straightforward partner awards) and is ready to unlock the next level of value.

    It has been revealed that the ideal profile: A couple or solo traveler planning a milestone trip — a significant anniversary, a sabbatical, a once-in-a-decade adventure — who wants to experience two destinations in business class without paying business class prices for either one. You're flexible on travel dates, comfortable spending time on the phone with an airline agent, and genuinely excited about the trip-planning process as part of the experience.

    It has been revealed that minimum points balance: You'll need approximately 80,000 Aeroplan miles to complete this booking (75,000 for the award plus 5,000 for the stopover). That's achievable from a single premium credit card welcome bonus, a combination of two or three mid-tier welcome bonuses, or 12–18 months of everyday spending on a 2x transferable points card.

    Pick a final destination and a stopover city on the same Star Alliance routing. Classic combos: Istanbul + Bangkok, Zurich + Tokyo, Vienna + Singapore. The stopover city must be a natural connection point on a Star Alliance route between your origin and destination.

    Sources indicate that set a calendar alert for 355 days before your departure date. Search for business class availability on each segment separately using United.com or Aeroplan.com. Both legs need saver-level award space on the same booking.

    Before transferring any points, verify that saver award space exists on both the outbound leg (origin to stopover city) and the continuation (stopover city to final destination). If either segment is unavailable, the booking will not work.

    Recent findings suggest that transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards (instant) or Amex Membership Rewards (1-2 days) to your Aeroplan account at a 1:1 ratio. Only transfer once you have confirmed availability on both segments.

    It has been revealed that call Aeroplan or use the multi-city search tool online. Specify your stopover city and duration (up to the maximum allowed). The system prices it as one round-trip award. Confirm total points match expectations before completing the booking.

    Aeroplan allows stopovers of up to 45 days on round-trip awards. You can stay in your stopover city for a few days or several weeks, giving you genuine time to explore rather than just passing through.

    In a recent development, no, stopovers are only available on round-trip awards through Aeroplan. One-way bookings do not qualify for the free stopover benefit. This is one reason round-trip awards can offer better value than two one-ways.

    It has been revealed that aeroplan has improved its online multi-city search tool, and some stopover itineraries can now be booked online. However, complex routings may still require a phone call. When calling, clearly state you want a round-trip award with a stopover and specify your stopover city and dates.

    The best stopover cities are Star Alliance hub cities with strong business class availability: Istanbul (Turkish Airlines hub), Zurich (SWISS hub), Vienna (Austrian hub), Singapore (Singapore Airlines hub), and Tokyo (ANA hub). These hubs offer the most consistent saver-level award space.

    According to recent reports, this sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

    According to recent reports, the Aeroplan stopover is one of the most powerful tools in the travel rewards playbook. By adding a free stopover to a round-trip business class award, you can explore two world-class cities for the points cost of visiting one. It requires planning, patience at the 355-day booking window, and comfort with Star Alliance routing rules, but the payoff is extraordinary: 10-15 cents per point in value on experiences that would cost thousands in cash. For the FI community member who has mastered basic award bookings and is ready to level up, this is the redemption that changes how you think about travel.

    #136977. Kids’ Clothes on Clearance – Buy Next Year’s Size, Not This Year’s

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (425 w)

    Kids’ Clothes on Clearance – Buy Next Year’s Size, Not This Year’s

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (425 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • New kids’ clothes cost the least at end-of-season clearance, but your child’s current size likely won’t fit when that season comes back.
    • It has been revealed that the biggest markdowns come twice a year.
    • In a recent development, you can predict next year’s size.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    New kids’ clothes cost the least at end-of-season clearance, but your child’s current size likely won’t fit when that season comes back. Shop for next year instead, usually one size up, and bring a list of what each child still needs so the markdowns fill real gaps.

    It has been revealed that the biggest markdowns come twice a year. Stores clear winter coats and snow pants after the holidays, and swimsuits and shorts in July, to make room for the next season’s stock.

    In a recent development, you can predict next year’s size. From age 2 until adolescence, children usually grow about 2½ inches a year, according to Nemours KidsHealth. That’s about one size on a typical kids’ size chart.

    It has been revealed that say your child wears a size 4 this winter, and a size 5 coat and snow pants cost $35 on clearance in January or $90 at full price next October. Buying in January saves $55 on clothes your child will need either way.

    To find next year’s size, measure your child’s height, add 2½ inches, and look up that height on the brand’s own size chart, since sizes vary by brand. Babies grow faster, about 10 inches on average in their first year, so buy them the size labeled for the age they’ll be a year from now. Stretchy knits and adjustable waistbands still fit when your guess is a little off.

    Bring a list to the sale. Count what each child already has in next year’s size, including clothes with room to grow, hand-me-downs, and secondhand finds. Then write down only the gaps, such as a coat and two pairs of pants.

    Leave shoes and boots off the list and buy them when they’re needed. The American Podiatric Medical Association notes that a child’s shoe size may change every few months, and it advises measuring the feet before buying shoes.

    Store each purchase in a bin labeled with the size and season, and open that bin before you shop when the season comes back.

    From its humble beginnings in 2008 to today, Bitcoin’s history has been relatively short but very eventful. The original protocol for this popular digital currency was created in 2008 by Satoshi Nakamoto, believed to be a pseudonym for an unknown developer or group of developers.

    Nakamoto launched the Bitcoin network just a year later and began mining the currency— an estimated 1 million bitcoins were mined in the early years.

    The creator(s) of this first-of-its-kind asset developed the cryptocurrency in response to the Great Recession of 2007-2009, spurred by a distrust of the traditional banking system and concerns about its stability.

    Recent findings suggest that given the recent values of Bitcoin, it’s hard to believe the currency first started trading on exchanges in 2010 at under $0.10. Since then, it’s experienced astronomical growth and some pretty wild price swings.

    At its most recent high, one bitcoin was worth over $64,000—a far cry from trading for pennies in its earliest days.

Read on for insights on Bitcoin milestones, historical returns, and how its returns compare to those of other assets.

    Sources indicate that let’s say you bought one bitcoin on August, 3rd 2013, for $1,106.75, its price at the time. If you held that one bitcoin until August 3rd, 2023, it would’ve been worth $29,310.44, and your total ROI for the 10 years would be 2,546.8%.

    We’ll also assume you purchased one Bitcoin for this example. A single bitcoin was valued at $965.31 on August, 3rd, 2018, and its value climbed to $29,310.44 by August 2023. Using our calculation above, your total ROI for those five years would be 294.1%.

    Tech Report: School Lunch Can Cost 40 Cents or Nothing – Check Whether Your Kids Qualify

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (468 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Before you pay for or pack another school lunch, find out whether your kids can get free or reduced-price meals.
    • It has been revealed that A family of four earning $55,000 a year qualifies for reduced-price meals this school year, and a reduced-price lunch costs 40 cents at most.
    • The Agriculture Department publishes the income limits each year by household size, at 185% of the federal poverty line for reduced-price meals and 130% for free ones.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Before you pay for or pack another school lunch, find out whether your kids can get free or reduced-price meals. Your school or state may already feed every student free, and kids in families on SNAP food benefits get free meals automatically. Otherwise, fill out the school’s meal application each school year, or whenever your income drops.

    It has been revealed that A family of four earning $55,000 a year qualifies for reduced-price meals this school year, and a reduced-price lunch costs 40 cents at most. With two kids buying lunch every day of a 180-day school year, that family saves $936 by paying 40 cents instead of $3.00, the typical elementary lunch price in a School Nutrition Association survey.

    The Agriculture Department publishes the income limits each year by household size, at 185% of the federal poverty line for reduced-price meals and 130% for free ones. Kids whose families get SNAP food benefits or TANF cash assistance qualify for free meals regardless of income, as do children in foster care, in Head Start, or experiencing homelessness.

    Nine states make school meals free for all public school students: California, Colorado, Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Latest Mexico, New York, and Vermont. Elsewhere, many schools serve every student free breakfast and lunch, with no applications, under the federal Community Eligibility Provision.

    Start by asking your kids’ school whether meals are free for everyone there this year. If they aren’t, look for a letter saying your kids were approved through SNAP or another benefit, which schools must send when no application is needed.

    Otherwise, fill out the free and reduced-price meal application, one form for all your kids in the district. Turn it in any time during the school year, including right after a job loss or pay cut. File a new one every school year, since an approval expires no later than 30 school days into the next. Federal rules bar schools from posting or announcing approved kids’ names, or singling them out in the lunch line.

    Recent findings suggest that if you pay full price, add up what your packed lunches cost before assuming they’re cheaper. Deloitte’s 2026 school lunch index put its cheapest packed lunch, built around a peanut butter and jelly sandwich, at $4.89, against $3.00 for a typical elementary school lunch.

    #136967. Wow, have you seen the stock market lately?

    📅 25 Feb 2025 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2593 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mrmoneymustache ↗ Open Full Page

    Wow, have you seen the stock market lately?

    📅 25 Feb 2025 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2593 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • And by lately, I mean the past several years or more.
    • In a recent development, the value of the S&P 500 index of stocks, where most of us hopefully have a good chunk of our retirement savings stashed into index funds, is up about fifty seven percent in just the past two years.
    • This means that on a net worth basis, if you felt like you were only halfway to retirement as recently as the Covid Era, you may have suddenly blown right past the finish line.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    And by lately, I mean the past several years or more.

    In a recent development, the value of the S&P 500 index of stocks, where most of us hopefully have a good chunk of our retirement savings stashed into index funds, is up about fifty seven percent in just the past two years. And it has more than doubled in the past five.

    This means that on a net worth basis, if you felt like you were only halfway to retirement as recently as the Covid Era, you may have suddenly blown right past the finish line. And some of us who were already retired long before that, may find ourselves eyeing up expensive properties or engaging in other money-burning-a-hole-in-our-pocket behaviors.

    In a recent development, is this real? Or is it all a bubble or some other sort of financial illusion?

    As one reader recently asked me in an email:.

    In a recent development, “The market seems to be in a huge bubble right now due to all sorts of hype around Artificial Intelligence. Does this make it more vulnerable to a huge crash in the future, and will it affect my retirement?”.

    To answer this question, let’s take a closer look at our current somewhat unprecedented financial world and stock market. And to understand that properly, it helps to go back to the roots of what a stock is:.

    A stock is a magical business arrangement which is really just a much more convenient version of a rental house.

    When you own a rental house, you are entitled to collect rent. After you cover all the expenses related to the house, you get to keep the rest, and this amount is your profit.

    If the average sale price of rental houses in your area goes up but the tenant keeps paying you the same amount forever, it may look good on paper but it doesn’t really mean anything unless you sell the house. And then you’d just have to turn around and pay that same higher amount for a different rental house.

    Your paycheck remains unchanged unless you can make your little house rental business more profitable. So you might squeeze in a basement apartment, do some renovations, streamline expenses, or do other things to increase your net earnings.

    When you eventually sell that house to another investor, the price they are willing to pay should be based on that future stream of income.

    For example, if the house brings in $2000 per month ($24,000 each year) and the sale price is $240,000, the next investor is buying a business with a price-to-earnings ratio of 10, because 240k/24k=10.

    But if you manage to convince someone to hand over $480,000 for that same house, you’ve sold at a P/E of 20. This is a much better deal for you as the seller, but quite obviously a less rosy future for the investor buying it.

    Now back to the stock market. If you put $100,000 in the market in 2019 and reinvested the dividends, today you’d already have an astonishing $256,960 (a 157% gain on your original investment).

    But in that same time period, your share of company earnings from that $100,000 basket of stocks has only gone from $5290 to $7540 (a measly 42% gain) – information you can get from handy analysis sites like multpl.com.

    In other words, the Price-to-earnings ratio has risen from about 20 back then, to about 30 today.

    So as stock investors here in 2025, we’re just like rental house investors finding that house prices have more than doubled while rents are only up by a bit. Which makes the landlord business a lot less profitable, and we should expect exactly the same thing as stock investor: lower future profits as a percentage of our portfolio value.

    It has been revealed that that doesn’t mean it’s unprofitable to own either one of these things – stocks or rental houses. But it does mean that we should expect our future income from buying them at today’s higher price-to-earnings ratio should be lower than if we could get them on sale. It’s just basic math.

    According to recent reports, but Wait! What if the Earnings are Rising?

    It has been revealed that let’s say you’re considering a rental house which is a bit overpriced based on today’s rent, but you happen to know that a significant Apple campus is about to get built right nearby. At that point, you expect that rent will start climbing rapidly for many years to come. In this situation, you should be willing to pay more for those future earnings when you buy the house.

    Recent findings suggest that this is exactly why the price of an individual company’s stock will tend to rise when some good news comes out about the company. During the Covid era, people started buying more Peloton bikes so they could exercise at home, and investors (foolishly) believed this would be a permanent trend. So Peloton stock went way up. Later, reality sunk in that this was just a fad and Peloton sales returned back to normal levels, and so did the stock.

    Recent findings suggest that but what does it mean when the entire market goes up to much higher levels? Does it mean our entire economy is expected to grow much more quickly?

    In the case of the current stock market euphoria, not exactly. Because if you dig into the share prices of the 500 significant companies that make up our famous S&P 500 index, it turns out that almost all the recent growth – about three quarters of it – came from just the seven biggest companies, known as the Magnificent Seven: Apple, Nvidia, Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Facebook, and sometimes Tesla.

    Recent findings suggest that these are all high-flying, super profitable tech companies who have seen a lot of growth and hype recently, which has caused investors to get excited and bid up their share prices in hopes of even more future growth. Collectively, they make up over 25% of the entire market value ($17.66 trillion!) and have much more expensive P/E ratios than the rest of the market (a weighted average of about 45).

    If you exclude these seven biggest companies and just consider the remaining 493, you will find a P/E of only 20, which is more reasonable although still much higher than average.

    What this tells us is that while investors expect the overall US economy to be fairly healthy in the coming years, they expect the biggest tech companies to continue to enjoy much faster growth.

    What Does This Have To Do With Artificial Intelligence?

    Industry observers note that there’s one common theme in the substantial tech tech giant boom right now: recent advances in AI have surprised the business world as software is suddenly able to display human-like reasoning in a rapidly growing number of fields. And because of this, the entire business world is fired up into a frenzy.

    Six of those Magnificent Seven companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build preposterously large warehouses full of supercomputers, and the lucky seventh (NVidia) is on the receiving end of those billions since they make the supercomputers and the incredible demand allows them to charge insane prices while still shipping them out by the trainload.

    But that’s just the first level of this boom, the AI Infrastructure. As you move down the chain, every other industry hopes we have entered a fresh era of productivity and thus profits will grow faster than ever.

    Recent findings suggest that they may actually be right: You can now do things like feed in an entire novel or legal document or piece of code and ask the AI to answer detailed questions about the characters, or identify loopholes in the contract, or even find and fix bugs for you. AI can also drive cars, identify melanoma from photographs of your skin, design medications thousands of times better than what we’re used to, and even bring humanoid robot bodies to life as mechanical workers.

    The idea is that we’re on the verge of having an infinite workforce of highly intelligent AI employees who will work for us for free, eliminating the biggest constraint that humanity has had in the past: a finite supply of both intelligence and labor.

    It has been revealed that having followed the field in some detail for a while, I personally think all this will come true, although the timeline is uncertain. And the people bidding the share prices up to these levels obviously believe it too.

    In a recent development, but the question is, will the profits of these companies really come through at the levels they forecast? Or will there be surprises down the road: cost overruns, competition, or unexpected disasters as these newly smarter-than-us computers decide that they no longer want to be bossed around?

    And what if we end up with massive unemployment and resulting social upheaval if this amazing technology puts us all out of work, leaving only Sam Altman atop his personal mountain of $100 trillion dollars taunting the world forevermore with an annoyingly quiet monotone cackle?

    There’s Only One Real Answer: Nobody Really Knows!

    While the future is unknown, it can still be useful to use the past as a guide. After all, if you look at the history of US economic growth over time, it averages out to a surprisingly steady figure, decade after decade: about 3% after inflation.

    One thing I noticed when making this graph: recent decades have actually seen slower than average growth, which is even less reason for the stock market to be priced the way it is.

    So What Does it all Mean? Should We Do Anything About It?

    In a recent development, as I mentioned earlier, it’s still going to be profitable to own stocks for the long run, just a bit less profitable than those times when we got to buy our stocks on sale. Of course, there will be occasional manias and panics and crashes. But as always, it will be a losing game to try to time them – for example by selling all your stocks now and hoping to buy them at a cheaper price at some point in the future.

    And over the long run, even if stocks return to more typical valuations, the end result would be something like the yellow line in this graph:.

    Our economy will continue to grow and company earnings will grow along with it, but future investors might choose to pay a lower multiple for those earnings.

    Just like when you eventually sell that rental house, you shouldn’t expect someone to pay you a million dollars for a place that only brings in $3000 of rent.

    Final Thoughts And Alternative Strategies.

    It has been revealed that everything we’ve covered so far is talking about the entire US stock market as a whole. And that’s what I usually focus on most because I still think this country is a uniquely good place to run a business. But what about other investing options? It’s always fun to at least look around and understand the larger investing world.

    Sources indicate that for starters, there’s Vanguard itself, the bedrock of the index fund world. Every year they gaze out at the investing horizon and make a ten-year forecast (guess) at future returns. This year they came up with these numbers:.

    Vanguard’s updated 10-year annualized return projections:.

    Wow look at that. Vanguard is forecasting that International stocks of all kinds and even bonds will outperform US stocks in the coming decade.

    On the surface, this makes sense because the P/E ratio of the international stocks (for example the VXUS fund) is only 15.9, meaning those European stocks are on sale at almost 50% off compared to ours!

    Sources indicate that just one note of caution however: Vanguard has been making this same prediction for several years and just been wrong so far. Part of the reason is that most of the AI boom seems to be happening in the US.

    Longtime readers know that I’ve had a growing portion of my investments in a Betterment (robo-advisor) account over the past eleven years (see the ongoing report here). I decided to try this for precisely the reasoning above: by allocating money across more categories than just US stocks and automatically rebalancing, we should be able to see slightly higher returns with slightly lower volatility, and some tax advantages as well.

    So far, my experiment has drawn some heat because in retrospect, a US-only portfolio has outperformed any other option over this time period. The Betterment portfolio comes close, but the exposure to bonds and businesses in other countries has held it back, just as you’d expect. But if you believe that things will eventually balance out again in the coming decades as the Vanguard analysis suggests above, it still has a chance to catch up.

    Looking at my investments there, you can review the betterment core portfolio and calculate that the weighted average of all those holdings gives us a P/E ratio of about 22.

    According to recent reports, it’s always worth checking in with The Oracle on matters of the economy while we’ve still got this wonderful old sage around (see this year’s Berkshire Hathaway Shareholder letter if you want some further deep reading). And Warren is signaling that things are overvalued and bargains are few and far between. So Berkshire is holding $334 billion of uninvested cash for now, not even repurchasing its own shares which it considers slightly overvalued at the current P/E ratio which averages out to about 21 in recent years.

    What About Paying Off Your House?

    Over the long run, you usually do better if you keep a mortgage on your house and pay it off slowly, while directing all the surplus cash into index funds. But there is some point at which the opposing factors of lower expected stock returns and higher interest rates meet in the middle and this situation flips.

    It has been revealed that if you have a 7% mortgage right now, it might be a fairly close tradeoff at this point. But the real factor is how you feel about paying off your house. I happen to love being mortgage-free so I paid off my last mortgage over ten years ago and have never looked back.

    It has been revealed that another way to think of this is that paying off your house is like buying a 7% bond. Definitely one of the best guaranteed returns around, and much more sensible than leaving tens of thousands of dollars in a checking or savings account unless you have a clear use for that cash.

    If you’ve read any of my stock investing articles before, you’ll know that we always end up at the same place: Just relax, enjoy your life, keep investing, ignore the daily news headlines* and don’t worry.

    Then reinvest that time that everyone else spends worrying into enjoying more time engaged in hard physical stuff in the great outdoors. That’s the only place where you’ll get guaranteed market-beating returns, every time.

    In the Comments: what are your thoughts on the current stock market boom, future crashes and busts, and the role of Artificial Intelligence in our future?

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If you work and earn a low or moderate income, check whether you can claim the earned income tax credit (EITC) every year before you file.
    • It has been revealed that about one in five workers who qualify for the EITC don’t claim it, by the IRS’s estimate.
    • In a recent development, your earned income from work and your adjusted gross income (AGI), which counts your other income too, must both fall under the IRS’s income limit for your filing status and how many qualifying children you claim.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If you work and earn a low or moderate income, check whether you can claim the earned income tax credit (EITC) every year before you file. A pay cut, a new baby, or a divorce can change the answer. The credit is refundable, so it pays you even if you owe no tax.

    It has been revealed that about one in five workers who qualify for the EITC don’t claim it, by the IRS’s estimate. The credit is worth up to $8,231 to a family with three or more children and up to $664 to a worker with none.

    In a recent development, your earned income from work and your adjusted gross income (AGI), which counts your other income too, must both fall under the IRS’s income limit for your filing status and how many qualifying children you claim. The IRS adjusts the limits for inflation each year. You also need investment income under a yearly cap and a valid Social Security number for you, a spouse on a joint return, and each child you claim. Without a qualifying child, you or a joint-filing spouse must be 25 to 64 at year’s end.

    Take a single parent with two qualifying children and no income but her pay, which came to $28,000 in 2026. By our math from the IRS’s 2026 figures, her credit is about $6,450.

    Sources indicate that start with the IRS’s EITC Assistant, which says whether you qualify and estimates your credit. To claim it, file Form 1040, adding Schedule EIC if you claim a qualifying child. Even if your pay was too low to require a return, file anyway to collect it. Your 2026 return may also need the IRS’s fresh Schedule 3-A, which asks whether you want your “federal public benefit,” the refunded part of your credits. Answer yes.

    Sources indicate that IRS-certified volunteers at Volunteer Income Tax Assistance (VITA) sites, which mainly serve workers who meet the EITC’s income guidelines, prepare basic returns free. The IRS’s VITA Locator finds sites near you.

    It has been revealed that by law, the IRS holds the entire refund on any return claiming the EITC until mid-February. The parent above, filing early online with direct deposit and no concerns on her return, can expect hers by early March, under the IRS’s schedule.

    Use Form 1040-X to claim the credit on any earlier return you filed without it, within three years of that return’s due date.

    Filers who’d rather prepare their own return can compare the best free tax software.

    In a recent development, an accredited investor is an individual or a business entity that is allowed to trade securities that may not be registered with financial authorities.     The concept of an accredited investor originated from the idea that individuals or entities with a higher financial acumen or more resources are better equipped to understand and bear the risks of certain investment opportunities.

    Historically, the distinction between accredited and non-accredited investors was established to protect less experienced investors from potentially risky or less transparent investment opportunities.

    Regulatory bodies, such as the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), have set criteria to determine who qualifies as an accredited investor, ensuring that they have the financial stability and sophistication to engage in more complex investment ventures.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, buy Travel Guard within 15 days of your first trip payment if a pre-existing condition, like heart disease or diabetes, could cancel your trip. Its three intends with cancellation coverage then cover that condition at no extra cost, as long as you insure all your nonrefundable trip costs and are well enough to travel when you buy.

    Sources indicate that travel Guard, which Zurich Insurance Group bought from AIG in 2024, sells three such plans: Essential, Preferred, and Deluxe. Without the pre-existing condition waiver, a initiative won’t pay for a condition, yours or a relative’s, that worsened, needed treatment, or changed medication in the 180 days before you buy (90 on Deluxe).

    Recent findings suggest that travel Guard suits travelers with a chronic condition, or a relative with one, who can buy within 15 days of their first trip payment, and parents bringing a child 17 or younger. A traveler with no such condition in the family gets nothing from the waiver and should first check the trip cancellation coverage on the card they booked with.
